def overlay(
    hists: list[Histogram],
    labels: list[str] | None = None,
    max_lines: int = 40,
    *,
    ratio: bool = False,
    ratio_lines: int = 10,
) -> str:
    """Overlay multiple 1D histograms and render as a unicode string.

    Cells where two or more histograms are present at the same height
    are rendered with a composite glyph (e.g. ○ + ✚ → ⊕).

    When *ratio* is ``True`` and at least two histograms are given, a ratio
    panel is appended below the main plot.  The ratio = 1 row is drawn as a
    dotted reference line (``·``); when a symbol lands exactly on that row it
    replaces the dot.

    Args:
        hists:       1D histograms to overlay.  At most 4 are supported, and
                     all must have exactly identical bin edges.
        labels:      Optional legend labels, one per histogram.
        max_lines:   Height of the plot area in terminal rows (minimum 5).
        ratio:       When ``True``, append a ratio panel (requires ≥ 2 hists).
        ratio_lines: Height of the ratio panel in rows (minimum 4).

    Returns:
        A multi-line unicode string.  Pass it to ``print()`` to display.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If any histogram is not 1D, the histograms have
                    different bin edges, negative values, invalid data,
                    more than 4 are supplied, or ``labels`` length does not match.
    """
    if not hists:
        raise ValueError('hists must not be empty')
    for hist in hists:
        hist.validate()
        if np.any(hist.values < 0):
            raise ValueError("Terminal backend requires nonnegative bin values")
        hists[0].require_compatible_binning(hist)
    if any(h.ndim != 1 for h in hists):
        raise ValueError('Terminal backend only supports 1D histograms')
    if len(hists) > 4:
        raise ValueError('Terminal backend supports at most 4 overlaid histograms')
    if labels is not None and len(labels) != len(hists):
        raise ValueError('labels must have the same length as hists')

    n_bins = len(hists[0].axes[0].edges) - 1
    if n_bins > MAX_BINS:
        raise ValueError(
            f'Terminal backend supports at most {MAX_BINS} bins, got {n_bins}'
        )

    return render(
        values_list=[h.values for h in hists],
        edges=hists[0].axes[0].edges,
        max_lines=max_lines,
        title=hists[0].title or '',
        x_label=hists[0].axes[0].label or '',
        labels=labels,
        ratio=ratio,
        ratio_lines=ratio_lines,
    )

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
unrooted ships a unrooted command that lets you load and plot ROOT histograms directly from the shell — no Python script required.

unrooted --input file.root --draw hist:hx --output plot.png

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The command is registered automatically when the package is installed. Follow Getting Started, or run from a source checkout:

python -m pip install .
# or
uv sync --no-dev

After a pip installation, unrooted --help should be available on your PATH. With uv, use uv run unrooted --help and prefix the commands below with uv run.

docs.title: Single histogram
docs.text:
unrooted \
  --input data.root \
  --draw hist:hx \
  --output hx.png

docs.title: Overlay with ratio panel
docs.text:
unrooted \
  --input data.root \
  --draw hist:hx hist:hy \
  --label "signal" "background" \
  --add ratio \
  --output overlay.svg

docs.title: Profile histogram from a subdirectory
docs.text:
unrooted \
  --input data.root \
  --source SeedingPerformance \
  --draw prof:nSeeds:eta \
  --add spread_continuous \
  --palette sd \
  --output profile.png

The --source prefix is prepended to every key, so the full ROOT path above is SeedingPerformance/nSeeds/eta. Colons inside the key path act as path separators, so prof:nSeeds:eta and prof:nSeeds/eta are equivalent.

docs.title: Efficiency histogram
docs.text:
unrooted \
  --input eff.root \
  --draw eff:h_passed:h_total \
  --title "Track reconstruction efficiency" \
  --output eff.svg

docs.title: Overlay the same key from multiple files
docs.text:
When multiple --input files are given with a single --draw spec, each file is loaded separately and overlaid. The filename stem is used as the label.

unrooted \
  --input run1.root run2.root run3.root \
  --draw hist:hx \
  --add ratio \
  --output comparison.png

docs.title: TTree branch
docs.text:
unrooted \
  --input data.root \
  --draw branch:myTree:eta \
  --n-bins 50 \
  --output eta.png

Profile from two branches:

unrooted \
  --input data.root \
  --draw branch:myTree:prof:eta:pt \
  --add spread_band \
  --output eta_vs_pt.png

docs.title: Scatter plot from a TTree
docs.text:
unrooted \
  --input data.root \
  --draw branch:myTree:scatter:v_eta:t_X0 \
  --output scatter.png

The plotly backend is also supported for scatter plots, enabling interactive zoom and hover:

unrooted \
  --input data.root \
  --draw branch:myTree:scatter:v_eta:t_X0 \
  --backend plotly \
  --output scatter.html

docs.title: Terminal backend
docs.text:
Useful for quick inspection in headless or SSH environments:

unrooted --input data.root --draw hist:hx --backend terminal

docs.title: Draw spec format
docs.text:
The --draw argument takes one or more draw specs separated by spaces or repeated --draw flags. Both forms are equivalent:

--draw hist:hx hist:hy
--draw hist:hx --draw hist:hy

docs.title: Spec syntax
docs.text:
Spec Loads via Auto style hist:key load(file, key) as_hist() th2:key load(file, key) as_hist() (2D heatmap) prof:key load(file, key) as_profile() eff:pass_key:total_key load_efficiency(file, pass, total) as_efficiency() branch:tree:x_branch load_branch(file, tree, x) as_hist() branch:tree:prof:x:y load_branch(file, tree, x, y) as_profile() branch:tree:scatter:x:y load_scatter(file, tree, x, y) as_scatter()

Type aliases: hist = th1 = h1; th2 = h2; prof = profile = tprofile; eff = efficiency; branch = tree.

Path separators inside a key can be / (ROOT convention) or : — both are converted to /:

--draw prof:dir/subdir/hist     # explicit slash
--draw prof:dir:subdir:hist     # colons → joined as dir/subdir/hist

docs.title: --source
docs.text:
--source KEY prepends a common path prefix to every histogram key. Useful when all objects live under the same ROOT directory:

unrooted --input f.root --source MyDir --draw hist:h1 hist:h2
# loads MyDir/h1 and MyDir/h2

--source is not prepended to the tree name in branch: specs. Use an explicit path such as branch:MyDir/tree:scatter:x:y for a nested tree. Leading and trailing slashes on the source prefix are normalized.

docs.title: Multi-file × multi-draw rules
docs.text:
--input count --draw count Behaviour 1 N load N histograms from the single file N 1 load the same key from every file; label = filename stem N N zip: (file_i, draw_i) N M ≠ N, M > 1 error

For one file or zipped files/specs, labels use the final draw key component (the passed key for efficiencies, the x branch for counts, or the y branch for profiles/scatter). For multiple files and one spec, filename stems take priority over the loaded histogram name. --label overrides these defaults and must supply exactly one label per dataset, including single-dataset plots.

docs.title: --add options
docs.text:
--add tokens modify the plot after the auto-style is chosen. They can be space-separated, colon-joined, or spread across multiple --add flags:

--add ratio spread_continuous           # two tokens, one flag
--add ratio:spread_continuous           # colon-joined, identical result
--add ratio --add spread_continuous     # two flags, identical result
Token Effect ratio ratio panel below main plot (all histogram backends; at least two 1D histograms) error_bar error display mode → bar caps at bin centres error_band error display mode → step-shaped filled band error_continuous error display mode → smooth filled band error_none suppress error display spread_bar spread display mode → bar caps spread_band spread display mode → step-shaped filled band spread_continuous spread display mode → smooth filled band spread_none suppress spread display

Choose at most one error_* mode and one spread_* mode. Conflicting modes raise an argument error; order does not select a winner. Ratios require exactly matching edges. Matplotlib and Plotly ratios inherit the numerator's line, marker, and error settings; spread and main-panel fill are not propagated to ratios. --add error_none suppresses ratio errors as well as main errors. Scatter plots have no ratio, error, or spread display.

Override the auto-selected style preset:

Preset Based on hist HistogramStyle.as_hist() — fill + error bars line HistogramStyle.as_line() — step line only markers HistogramStyle.as_markers() — markers + errors efficiency HistogramStyle.as_efficiency() — markers + spread band profile HistogramStyle.as_profile() — line + spread band scatter HistogramStyle.as_scatter() — tiny point markers

Name Description odd (default) OpenDataDetector: steel blue, orange, teal, crimson sd Super Duper: teal, purple, pink, yellow

Colors cycle automatically across multiple histograms.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
--backend Output Notes mpl (default) matplotlib figure saved with --output; supports .png/.svg/.pdf plotly interactive HTML/image .html for interactive; install the optional Plotly backend as described in Getting Started terminal unicode to stdout no output file; --max-lines N controls height Capability / option Matplotlib Plotly Terminal Single 1D histogram / overlay / ratio Yes Yes Yes, up to 4 datasets and 100 bins Single 2D heatmap Yes Yes Unsupported Scatter / scatter overlay Yes Yes Unsupported Error and spread display Yes Yes Omitted; explicit display requests rejected Title, x label, legend labels Yes Yes Yes Y label and axis limits Yes Yes Unsupported Style, palette, marker, line overrides Yes Yes Unsupported Fixed ratio y range Yes Yes Unsupported --output / --show Yes Yes Unsupported; writes to stdout --max-lines Unsupported Unsupported Integer ≥ 5

Single 2D heatmaps accept title, axis labels, and limits, but do not accept --label, --add, or 1D style overrides. Scatter supports --style scatter and marker overrides; line styles and histogram style presets are rejected. --n-bins and --branch-range require a count/profile branch spec. Ranges must be finite with MIN < MAX, and --n-bins must be positive. Unsupported combinations raise an error instead of silently discarding flags.

Plotly HTML output is self-contained and needs only the Plotly extra. Static images additionally need Kaleido; Kaleido 1+ requires a compatible installed Chrome or Chromium. See Plotly's export setup. These optional tools are not installed by unrooted[plotly]. Export failures identify the destination and suggest HTML when the static export setup fails.

docs.title: Output and display
docs.text:
Flags Behaviour --output FILE save figure to file --show open interactive window even when --output is given (neither) open interactive window (equivalent to --show)

These display rules apply to graphical backends. Terminal output always goes to stdout; redirect it with your shell to save a text preview.

For branch draw specs, use --entry-start N and --entry-stop N to select tree entries before broadcasting or flattening. The start is included and the stop is excluded; defaults are zero and the end of the tree. Bounds are nonnegative, ordered, and clipped to the tree length. The selection applies independently to each input file. These flags are rejected when the command has no branch spec; stored histograms are unaffected.

unrooted --input data.root --draw branch:tree:scatter:x:y \
  --entry-start 1000 --entry-stop 2000 --output selected.png

--step-size N sets the maximum tree entries per chunk (default 100000); it requires a branch spec and is not a byte limit. For scatter datasets, --max-points N explicitly limits retained flattened pairs per dataset. The default policy --sampling error fails on overflow. Select uniform sampling explicitly, with a repeatable nonnegative seed:

unrooted --input data.root --draw branch:tree:scatter:x:y \
  --max-points 100000 --sampling random --seed 71 \
  --step-size 100000 --backend plotly --output sampled.html

--sampling random requires --max-points; --seed requires random sampling and defaults to 0. Sampling flags are rejected for histogram/profile specs. No sampling happens without an explicit request. When points are removed, the CLI reports retained/source pair counts and the seed on stderr. Point counts are after event selection and broadcasting; returned points remain in input order. See loading memory and sampling for the memory model, statistical meaning, and reference measurements.

With ratios, --xlabel applies to the bottom axis and --ylabel / --ylim apply to the main panel. --ratio-range controls only the ratio y-axis and requires --add ratio. --xlim applies to the shared x range.

docs.title: Errors and exit codes
docs.text:
Exit code Meaning 0 Successful rendering/export, or --help 2 Invalid syntax, conflicting flags, or an unsupported option combination 1 Loading, plotting, optional dependency, display, or export failure

Errors go to stderr with an unrooted: prefix and no traceback. Missing files/keys and unsupported ROOT objects are loading errors. For example, th2: with a 1D object or prof: with a plain count histogram fails clearly. Invalid file/spec combinations and label counts are argument errors. Long options must be spelled in full; the CLI does not accept abbreviations.

docs.title: The Histogram dataclass
docs.text:
Histogram is the central data structure. It is a plain Python dataclass — no magic, no hidden state — so you can always work with its arrays directly.

from unrooted.core.histogram import Histogram
from unrooted.core.axis import Axis
import numpy as np

edges = np.linspace(0, 10, 11)   # 10 bins
values = np.array([1,3,5,8,10,9,7,4,2,1], dtype=float)

h = Histogram(
    axes=[Axis(edges=edges, label="x [cm]")],
    values=values,
    variances=values.copy(),   # Poisson: Var(N) = N
    name="my_hist",
)

docs.title: Key attributes
docs.text: Attribute Type Description axes list[Axis] One per dimension values ndarray Bin contents variances ndarray Per-bin variance errors ndarray (property) sqrt(variances) ndim int (property) Number of dimensions name str Optional identifier title str Optional longer title overflow ndarray \| None Values with flow bins spread_min ndarray \| None Optional lower spread bound; meaning depends on the reader spread_max ndarray \| None Optional upper spread bound; meaning depends on the reader

docs.title: Validation and missing data
docs.text:
Construction raises ValueError for invalid data. An axis must have at least two finite, strictly increasing, one-dimensional numeric edges; edges are converted to float64. A histogram needs at least one axis, and values and variances must have shape (axis_0.n_bins, axis_1.n_bins, ...). Variances must be nonnegative. Boolean, complex, string, and object arrays are rejected.

Values may be negative, for example after a weighted fill. Histogram arrays may contain NaN to mark missing data or uncertainty; infinity is rejected. Spread bounds must be supplied together, match the values' shape, have paired NaN positions, be ordered, and enclose the central values wherever both are defined. Sparse profiles may therefore have a finite value and NaN spread.

ScatterData(x, y) follows the same numeric rules and requires flat arrays of equal length. Empty arrays and NaN gaps are allowed.

Tree readers also attach scatter provenance: source_points is the selected flattened count, sample_seed records an explicitly requested random sampler, and the sampled property indicates whether fewer pairs were retained. Manually created objects may leave those optional fields unset. See scatter limits and sampling.

docs.title: Ownership and mutation
docs.text:
Core constructors use np.asarray; they borrow arrays when conversion is unnecessary. Mutating an input array can change the object, and axis objects are shared. Use .copy() on your inputs when you need isolation. Readers return independent snapshots of their source data. Histogram values, variances, and flow arrays from readers do not share storage with each other.

Objects remain mutable. Call h.validate() or scatter.validate() after editing their arrays or axes. Public plotting functions validate again before drawing. Validation does not recompute variances, spread, or flow contents after a value is changed; updating related quantities remains your responsibility.

docs.title: Flow bins
docs.text:
values and variances exclude flow bins. If present, overflow is a full values array of shape (n_0 + 2, n_1 + 2, ...): index 0 on each axis is underflow, indices 1:-1 are ordinary bins, and the final index is overflow. This includes multidimensional corner flows. It stores contents, not flow variances, and plotting uses only values.

ROOT readers populate both flow slots per axis. Boost readers pad disabled flow slots with NaN, distinguishing unavailable data from an observed zero. Branch readers set overflow=None and omit out-of-range observations. Flow arrays are snapshots and do not synchronize with later edits to values.

docs.title: Profile histograms
docs.text:
When load_branch() returns a profile histogram, spread_min and spread_max hold the per-bin extreme values of the profiled quantity. Empty bins have np.nan in both spread arrays.

For N > 0 observations, branch-profile variances use sum((y - mean(y))**2) / N², retaining the population convention. Empty bins have value and variance 0; single-entry bins have the observed value and variance 0. The spread bounds distinguish an empty bin from a populated bin whose values and variance happen to be zero.

Profiles loaded from ROOT TProfile or boost-histogram Mean storage instead carry mean ± standard deviation in these fields. Efficiency readers use them for interval bounds. These bands have different interpretations; consult the ROOT and boost-histogram loading guides when comparing them.

Boost Mean profiles retain sample-corrected variance sum((y - mean(y))**2) / (N * (N - 1)) for N >= 2. Matching profile means therefore do not imply matching error bars. ROOT TProfile variances are read through uproot.

from unrooted.io.root import load_branch

hp = load_branch("data.root", "tree", "x", "y")

import numpy as np
populated = ~np.isnan(hp.spread_min)
print("populated bins:", populated.sum())
print("mean range:", hp.values[populated].min(), "…", hp.values[populated].max())

docs.title: The Axis dataclass
docs.text:
Each Axis stores the bin edges for one dimension.

from unrooted.core.axis import Axis
import numpy as np

ax = Axis(edges=np.linspace(-3, 3, 61), label="η")

ax.n_bins    # 60
ax.centers   # array of 60 bin-centre coordinates
ax.widths    # array of 60 bin widths (uniform here: 0.1 each)

docs.title: Convenience aliases
docs.text:
from unrooted.core.histogram import Histogram1D, Histogram2D
# Both are just Histogram — provided for type-annotation clarity.

docs.title: Loading boost-histogram Data
docs.text: unrooted can convert boost-histogram objects directly into the common Histogram representation — no ROOT files involved. This is the recommended path when your analysis pipeline already produces boost_histogram.Histogram objects (e.g. from coffea or hand-filled histograms).

docs.title: Profile histograms (Mean storage)
docs.text:
A boost_histogram.Histogram with Mean storage is converted to the common profile representation. Its sample-corrected uncertainties and spread are described below.

import pickle
from unrooted.io.boost import load

with open("histograms.pkl", "rb") as f:
    data = pickle.load(f)          # dict of bh.Histogram objects

prof = load(data["nMeasurements_vs_eta"], name="nMeasurements_vs_eta")

The Mean storage provides three fields per bin; load() derives the standard quantities from them:

bh field Meaning Maps to count number of fills — value per-bin mean h.values _sum_of_deltas_squared Σ(x − mean)² → SE² and σ_y Attribute Content h.values Per-bin mean h.variances Per-bin SE² = Σ(x−mean)² / (N(N−1)) h.errors √SE² — standard error of the mean h.spread_min mean − σ_y (std-dev of individual measurements) h.spread_max mean + σ_y h.overflow mean values including under/overflow bins

σ_y = √(Σ(x−mean)² / (N−1)). Bins with count = 0 carry nan for the spread fields; bins with count = 1 carry σ_y = 0.

The SE² formula applies for N >= 2. This reader retains variance 0 for bins with zero or one observation; empty bins have value 0.

Unlike profiles computed from branches, which retain population SE² = Σ(x−mean)² / N², Mean storage uses the sample correction. For observations [1, 3], both readers return mean 2, but the branch variance is 0.5 and the boost variance is 1. Branch spread records observed extrema; boost spread is mean ± sample standard deviation.

Axis metadata strings (e.g. bh.axis.Variable([...], metadata="#eta")) become axis labels automatically.

from unrooted.plot.mpl import plot
from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle
from unrooted.plot.style_set import StyleSet

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")
plot(prof, style=HistogramStyle.as_profile().with_color(ss.colors[0]))

docs.title: Efficiency histograms
docs.text:
Pass a pair of count-storage histograms (accepted, total) to load_efficiency(). This mirrors the ROOT load_efficiency() API, but accepts in-memory objects rather than file paths.

from unrooted.io.boost import load_efficiency

# data["trackeff_vs_eta"] is {"accepted": bh.Histogram, "total": bh.Histogram}
eff_entry = data["trackeff_vs_eta"]
eff = load_efficiency(eff_entry["accepted"], eff_entry["total"], name="trackeff")
Attribute Content eff.values Per-bin efficiency = accepted / total eff.variances Binomial variance = eff × (1 − eff) / total eff.spread_min Lower Wilson interval bound eff.spread_max Upper Wilson interval bound

Both inputs must be 1D, with exactly identical edges and finite nonnegative integer counts satisfying accepted ≤ total. Supported count storages are Double, Int64, Unlimited, and AtomicInt64. Weight, Mean, and WeightedMean are rejected, including Weight filled with unit weights. Scalar inputs whose boost variance information is unknown after a weighted fill are also rejected. Manually assigned scalar contents cannot establish the history of weights; callers must supply unweighted counts. Fractional or weighted efficiencies are unsupported.

Bounds use the Wilson score interval without continuity correction, with confidence_level=0.6826894921370859 (68.27%) by default; pass confidence_level=0.95 for 95% intervals. This replaces the previous clamped Gaussian spread and retains p*(1-p)/N in variances. Zero-total bins carry NaN in all four arrays; flow bins are excluded. Invalid inputs or confidence levels outside (0, 1) raise ValueError. The ROOT efficiency guide gives the formula, endpoint examples, and the difference between Wilson bounds and errors.

from unrooted.plot.mpl import plot
from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle

plot(eff, style=HistogramStyle.as_efficiency().with_color(ss.colors[1]))

docs.title: Scalar and Weight storage
docs.text:
load() supports the scalar storages Double, Int64, Unlimited, and AtomicInt64, plus Weight and Mean. WeightedMean is explicitly unsupported; its weighted profile uncertainty is not yet defined here. Other storage types raise ValueError.

Double / Int64 (count histogram)Weight storage 
import boost_histogram as bh
from unrooted.io.boost import load

h = bh.Histogram(bh.axis.Regular(50, -5, 5))
h.fill(data)

hist = load(h, name="x_dist")
# hist.variances == hist.values  (Poisson assumption)

h = bh.Histogram(bh.axis.Regular(50, -5, 5), storage=bh.storage.Weight())
h.fill(data, weight=weights)

hist = load(h, name="x_weighted")
# hist.values    → Σw  per bin
# hist.variances → Σw² per bin
Storage type h.values h.variances spread_min/max Double / Int64 / Unlimited / AtomicInt64 bin count = values (Poisson) None Weight Σw per bin Σw² per bin None Mean per-bin mean SE² per bin mean ± σ_y

docs.title: Numeric axes
docs.text:
Regular, Variable, and Integer axes are supported; edges are extracted via the .edges property. Categorical (IntCategory, StrCategory) and Boolean axes raise ValueError because the core representation does not preserve their category semantics. Numeric axes must yield finite, strictly increasing edges. Transformed, growing, and circular numeric axes are stored as a static snapshot of their current edges and contents; later growth or wrapping behavior belongs to the original boost histogram.

# Variable bin widths
ax = bh.axis.Variable([-4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4], metadata="η")

# Uniform bins
ax = bh.axis.Regular(40, -4, 4, metadata="η")

The metadata field of each axis becomes the Axis.label string in the returned Histogram.

All returned arrays are independent snapshots. overflow always includes both flow slots per axis; disabled flow slots are padded with NaN. See the core data contract for shape and mutation semantics.

docs.title: Multi-dimensional histograms
docs.text:
load() handles any number of axes — a 2D histogram produces a Histogram with ndim = 2 and two Axis objects, just like a ROOT TH2:

h2d = bh.Histogram(
    bh.axis.Regular(40, -4, 4, metadata="η"),
    bh.axis.Regular(60, -3.14, 3.14, metadata="φ"),
)
h2d.fill(eta, phi)

hist2d = load(h2d, name="eta_phi")
# hist2d.ndim == 2
# hist2d.values.shape == (40, 60)

docs.title: ROOT histograms
docs.text:
Use load() to read any TH1, TH2, or TProfile object directly from a ROOT file. No ROOT installation is needed — unrooted uses uproot under the hood.

from unrooted.io.root import load

h = load("analysis.root", "hx")

The key can include or omit the ROOT cycle number:

h = load("analysis.root", "hx")    # cycle stripped automatically
h = load("analysis.root", "hx;1")  # explicit cycle – same result

docs.title: What gets loaded
docs.text: Attribute Content h.values Bin contents as np.ndarray h.variances Bin variances (sumw2 if stored, else values) h.axes One Axis per dimension with edges and label h.overflow Full array including flow bins h.name Key string (cycle stripped)

docs.title: TProfile
docs.text:
When the loaded object is a TProfile, load() additionally populates:

Attribute Content h.values Per-bin mean of the profiled quantity h.variances Per-bin squared standard error of the mean (SE²) h.spread_min Per-bin mean − σ_y (std-dev of profiled quantity) h.spread_max Per-bin mean + σ_y

σ_y is derived as √(SE² × N) from the stored SE² and bin counts. Empty bins carry nan for the spread fields.

hp = load("analysis.root", "profX")

# hp.values      → per-bin mean
# hp.variances   → per-bin SE² (error bars via hp.errors)
# hp.spread_min  → mean − σ_y  (spread band)
# hp.spread_max  → mean + σ_y

Plot with a spread band:

from unrooted.plot.mpl import plot
from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle

style = HistogramStyle(
    line_color="#1A4F8A",
    error_display="bar",    # SE error bars
    spread_display="band",  # σ_y shaded band
)
plot(hp, style=style)

docs.title: Efficiency histograms
docs.text:
Direct TEfficiency loading is unsupported. Use load_efficiency() with a passed and a total TH1 stored as separate keys — a common pattern in analysis frameworks:

from unrooted.io.root import load_efficiency

eff = load_efficiency("analysis.root", "h_passed", "h_total")
Attribute Content eff.values Per-bin efficiency = passed / total eff.variances Per-bin binomial variance = eff × (1 − eff) / total eff.spread_min Lower Wilson interval bound eff.spread_max Upper Wilson interval bound

The default confidence level is 0.6826894921370859 (68.27%, equivalent to the central Gaussian ±1σ probability). Pass confidence_level=0.95 for 95% intervals. The method is the Wilson score interval without continuity correction. It replaces the previous clamped Gaussian spread; the binomial variance field is unchanged. No additional statistical dependency is required.

For N > 0, p = passed/N, and the standard-normal quantile z at (1 + confidence_level)/2, the bounds are

center = (p + z²/(2N)) / (1 + z²/N)
radius = z * sqrt(p*(1-p)/N + z²/(4N²)) / (1 + z²/N)
bounds = center ± radius

Bounds lie in [0, 1] and retain nonzero width at zero and full acceptance. At the default confidence level, 0/4 has bounds [0, 0.2], 2/4 has bounds approximately [0.276393, 0.723607], and 4/4 has bounds [0.8, 1]. Bins where total = 0 carry nan for all four arrays; no inference is made from an empty bin.

errors = sqrt(variances) still describes the Gaussian binomial standard error and is zero at the endpoints. To show Wilson bounds, enable spread_display; changing the confidence level affects only the bounds.

from unrooted.plot.mpl import plot
from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle

style = HistogramStyle(
    line_color="#1A4F8A",
    marker="o",
    error_display=None,
    spread_display="band",  # shaded Wilson interval
)
plot(eff, style=style)

Inputs must be one-dimensional TH1 count histograms with exactly identical edges. Counts must be finite, nonnegative integers, with passed ≤ total in every bin. Weighted and fractional efficiencies are unsupported. ROOT variances must match counts (relative tolerance 1e-12); a stored Sumw2 array with unit-weight Poisson variances is accepted. ROOT cannot always establish the history of weights from aggregated counts, so callers must supply unweighted event counts. Profiles and TH2 inputs are rejected. Invalid data or a confidence level outside (0, 1) raises ValueError. Flow bins are excluded from the efficiency calculation.

docs.title: TTree branches
docs.text: load_branch() reads one or two branches from a TTree and returns a histogram.

docs.title: Count histogram (one branch)
docs.text:
from unrooted.io.root import load_branch

h = load_branch("data.root", "tree", "x")
# → Histogram with 100 bins, range auto-detected from data

Options:

h = load_branch("data.root", "tree", "x",
                n_bins=50,
                range=(-5.0, 5.0),
                label="x [mm]")

Count and profile histograms use bins [left, right), with the final right edge included in the last bin. A value exactly on an internal edge belongs to the bin on its right. Values outside the specified range are omitted.

docs.title: Entry selection
docs.text:
Both load_branch() and load_scatter() accept a half-open tree-entry slice:

from unrooted.io.root import load_branch, load_scatter

h = load_branch("data.root", "tree", "x", entry_start=1000, entry_stop=2000)
points = load_scatter("data.root", "tree", "x", "y",
                      entry_start=1000, entry_stop=2000)

entry_start defaults to 0; entry_stop=None reads through the end of the tree. Bounds must be nonnegative integers with stop ≥ start; bounds beyond the tree's length are clipped. Selection happens before broadcasting and flattening, so the bounds count events, not flattened points. All elements of a selected jagged event are included. Automatic histogram ranges use only the selected x values, before broadcasting. An empty selection needs an explicit histogram range; it returns an empty scatter without a range.

docs.title: Profile histogram (two branches)
docs.text:
Provide y_branch to profile y values against x-axis bins. Each x-bin stores the mean, standard error, and min/max of the corresponding y values.

hp = load_branch("data.root", "tree", "x", "y")
# hp.values     → per-bin mean of y
# hp.variances  → per-bin SE² of mean
# hp.spread_min → per-bin minimum of y
# hp.spread_max → per-bin maximum of y

For a bin with N > 0 observations, define M2 = sum((y - mean(y))**2). Branch profiles use the population convention:

values    = mean(y)
variances = M2 / N²
errors    = sqrt(variances)

This is the population variance of the observations divided by N; it does not apply the sample correction N / (N - 1). For observations [1, 3], the mean is 2, the variance of the mean is 0.5, and the spread bounds are [1, 3]. The calculation centers values within each bin before accumulating squared deviations, avoiding cancellation from a large common offset.

Entries in a bin Value Variance Spread bounds 0 0 0 both nan 1 observed value 0 both equal to the observation 2 or more mean M2 / N² observed minimum and maximum

The zero variance for a single observation preserves the existing convention; it does not establish that the underlying distribution has no uncertainty. An entirely empty tree can be loaded with an explicit range=(lo, hi); automatic range detection needs at least one x-value.

The boost-histogram Mean reader retains its sample-corrected variance M2 / (N * (N - 1)) for N >= 2 and mean ± standard deviation spread. Those uncertainty and spread definitions differ from branch profiles even when the means and binning agree.

docs.title: Supported branch-pair types
docs.text:
load_branch() uses awkward.broadcast_arrays to align the two branches, supporting all common branch-shape combinations:

Case x type y type Behaviour 1 scalar scalar event-by-event pairing 2 scalar std::vector<T> x broadcast to every y element per event 3 scalar std::vector<std::vector<T>> x broadcast after full flattening 4 std::vector<T> std::vector<T> (same shape) element-by-element zip 5 std::vector<T> std::vector<std::vector<T>> outer lengths must match

Scalar, std::vector<T>, and std::vector<std::vector<T>> branches all work for count histograms too — they are fully flattened before binning.

Note

Incompatible branch shapes (e.g. different outer lengths) raise a ValueError from awkward-array.

docs.title: Chunking and memory
docs.text:
Branch readers process at most step_size=100_000 tree entries per chunk. Set a smaller positive integer to reduce temporary array sizes. Entry counts are measured before broadcasting/flattening: one jagged event may contain many points, and ROOT baskets also contribute memory. step_size is an entry limit, not a hard limit on process RAM.

Count histograms accumulate one chunk at a time. Profiles use three passes over the selection: extrema/counts, sums relative to a common per-bin origin, and centered squared deviations. The extra I/O retains the population estimator and large-offset stability while keeping working arrays bounded by the chunk and bin count. Automatic range detection adds an x-only pass; provide range=(lo, hi) to avoid that scan. Interpreted arrays are not cached between passes.

For count/profile output, result memory depends on the number of bins. Scatter output without max_points retains every selected pair, so its result memory still grows with the selection. Use an explicit limit when that result must be bounded.

docs.title: Scatter limits and sampling
docs.text:
from unrooted.io.root import load_scatter

# A guard: raise ValueError if the selection exceeds 100,000 flattened pairs.
points = load_scatter("data.root", "tree", "x", "y", max_points=100_000)

# An explicit uniform sample without replacement, with a reproducible seed.
sample = load_scatter("data.root", "tree", "x", "y",
                      max_points=100_000, sampling="random", seed=71,
                      step_size=100_000)
print(len(sample.x), sample.source_points, sample.sampled, sample.sample_seed)

The default max_points=None returns all pairs. Setting a limit defaults to sampling="error"; it never silently truncates. sampling="random" requires a positive limit and uses seed 0 by default. A limit at or above the selected pair count returns all pairs.

Sampling is uniform over flattened (x, y) pairs, including NaN gaps, rather than over events. High-multiplicity events contribute more pairs. Coordinates stay paired, selected points retain their original order, and the same input/selection, seed, and software versions give the same sample across chunk sizes. source_points records the selected flattened count; sampled is true only when fewer pairs were retained. sample_seed records the requested random seed. Working memory is proportional to a chunk plus the retained limit; the complete source selection is still scanned.

docs.title: Reference workload measurements
docs.text:
The Stage 5 target is 10 million flattened observations per histogram/profile, under 1 GiB peak process RAM and 30 seconds per load on the local reference workload. Scatter sampling is explicitly requested, with 100,000 retained points in the reference run. These targets are measured on synthetic local ROOT data, rather than a universal limit for every file or machine.

On arm64 macOS / Python 3.14.6, using 100 bins, an explicit range, and three fresh worker processes per case:

10-million-observation case Whole-branch median load Chunked median load Whole-branch peak RAM Chunked peak RAM Scalar count 0.468 s 0.534 s 262.5 MiB 74.0 MiB Jagged count 0.484 s 0.490 s 281.1 MiB 106.9 MiB Scalar profile 0.834 s 2.352 s 820.0 MiB 104.7 MiB Jagged profile 0.865 s 2.315 s 877.4 MiB 238.3 MiB

The jagged fixture has 10 observations per event. Profiles trade additional passes for lower memory while staying within the agreed time budget. Sampling 100,000 pairs from 10 million took median 0.52–0.61 s and at most 251.4 MiB during loading; self-contained Plotly HTML was 7.0 MiB. Rendering raised peak process RAM to at most 318.7 MiB for that sampled workload.

Reproduce from the source checkout (with development/Plotly dependencies):

uv run python -I benchmarks/root_loading.py \
  --workdir /tmp/unrooted-benchmark --observations 10000000 --repeat 3 \
  --step-size 100000 --max-points 100000 --render \
  --report /tmp/unrooted-benchmark/report.json

Add --auto-range to include the preliminary range scan. The benchmark generates seeded scalar/jagged fixtures and runs each load/export in a fresh subprocess. Reports record dependency versions, input and reader hashes, load/render time, result/output size, and peak RSS. Fixture generation is excluded; filesystem caches are not cleared. Peak values include interpreter and library memory. Raw before/after reports are in benchmarks/results/.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
unrooted ships three independent plotting backends that share the same Histogram, HistogramStyle, and StyleSet objects.

Backend Import Returns Best for matplotlib unrooted.plot.mpl matplotlib.axes.Axes publication figures, scripts plotly unrooted.plot.plotly plotly.graph_objects.Figure interactive exploration terminal unrooted.plot.terminal str quick inspection, headless environments, CI logs

docs.title: Matplotlib backend
docs.text: from unrooted.plot.mpl import plot, overlay

docs.title: plot() — single histogram
docs.text:
ax = plot(h)

By default plot() creates a new figure. Pass an existing ax to draw into it:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot(h, ax=ax)

docs.title: Unstyled (keyword-argument) mode
docs.text:
Any keyword is forwarded to the underlying matplotlib call. This is the "quick and dirty" path — convenient for exploration:

ax = plot(h, color="steelblue", linewidth=2, label="data")

docs.title: Styled mode
docs.text:
Pass a HistogramStyle (or get one from a StyleSet) for full control over line, marker, fill, error bars, and spread display:

from unrooted.plot import HistogramStyle

style = HistogramStyle(
    line_color="#1A4F8A",
    marker="o",
    fill_alpha=0.15,
    error_display="bar",
    spread_display="band",   # "bar", "band", or "continuous"
)
ax = plot(h, style=style)

Note

style= and **kwargs cannot be combined — pass one or the other.

docs.title: overlay() — multiple histograms
docs.text:
(ax_main, ax_ratio) = overlay(
    [h1, h2, h3],
    labels=["signal", "background", "data"],
    styles=[ss[0], ss[1], ss[2]],
)

overlay() always returns a tuple (ax_main, ax_ratio). When ratio=False (default), ax_ratio is None.

docs.title: Ratio panel
docs.text:
(ax, ax_r) = overlay([h1, h2], labels=["h1", "h2"], ratio=True)

The ratio panel shows h_i / h_0 for each subsequent histogram. Every backend requires exactly identical bin edges and dimensions for ratios; there is no automatic rebinning or approximate edge matching. Ordinary Matplotlib and Plotly overlays may use different grids when ratio=False.

Graphical ratio uncertainties use Gaussian propagation with independent inputs: for numerator B and reference A, Var(B/A) = Var(B)/A² + B² Var(A)/A⁴. No covariance is included. This does not describe a passed/total efficiency or another correlated ratio; use an efficiency reader for the supported binomial case. Zero reference bins are shown as NaN gaps. For A=10, B=5, and Poisson variances, the ratio is 0.5 and its propagated variance is 0.075.

Both graphical backends inherit the style of B in the ratio panel: line color, opacity, style, width, marker settings, and error display settings come from the numerator's HistogramStyle. line_style=None hides its ratio line; error_display=None hides its ratio errors. Error bars, step bands, and continuous bands follow the selected mode. Main-panel fill and spread bounds are omitted from ratios. Use LineStyle.DASHED to distinguish a ratio line:

from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle, LineStyle
from unrooted.plot.style_set import StyleSet

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")
sx = HistogramStyle.as_hist().with_color(ss.colors[0])              # reference
sy = HistogramStyle.as_line(line_style=LineStyle.DASHED,
                             line_width=2.0,
                             error_display="bar").with_color(ss.colors[1])  # B
overlay([hx, hy], ratio=True, labels=["ref", "B"], styles=[sx, sy])

docs.title: Passing an existing axes
docs.text:
overlay() accepts a single axes object and draws all histograms into it. A ratio panel cannot be added when an external ax is supplied.

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
overlay([h1, h2], ax=ax, labels=["h1", "h2"])

docs.title: stack() — additive histogram components
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot import HistogramStyle, StyleSet
from unrooted.plot.mpl import stack

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")
styles = [HistogramStyle.as_stack().with_color(c) for c in ss.colors[:3]]
ax = stack(
    [background_a, background_b, signal],
    labels=["Background A", "Background B", "Signal"],
    styles=styles,
)
ax.set_ylabel("Events / bin")
ax.figure.savefig("stack.png")

Components are drawn bottom to top in input order. All inputs must be 1D, have exactly identical bin edges, and contain nonnegative additive counts or yields. Weighted yields are supported when every bin is nonnegative. Profiles and efficiencies carrying spread bounds are rejected; do not stack averages, efficiencies, or other non-additive quantities. There is no automatic rebinning or normalization, and flow bins are omitted. Input arrays and styles are preserved.

By default a gray band shows the total ± sqrt(sum(variances)), assuming independent components. It includes no covariance and is not clipped at zero. For yields 4 and 9 with variances 4 and 9, the total is 13 ± √13. Pass uncertainty=False to hide it. A NaN value in any component leaves a gap in every layer of that bin. A NaN variance leaves a gap only in the total band.

stack() returns an Axes and accepts ax= for composition. labels and styles, when supplied, need one entry per component. The default HistogramStyle.as_stack() has a filled area and outline; the component's line and fill fields apply, while marker/error/spread fields do not. The total band is controlled by uncertainty. For palette colors, create as_stack() styles as above. Both backends support hatches /, \, x, -, |, +, and .; use hex/RGBA colors for consistent opacity across backends.

Reproduce this synthetic example from a contributor checkout:

uv run --no-sync python -I tests/examples/example_stacked_histogram.py /tmp/stack-example --plotly

Stacking is a Python API feature of Matplotlib and Plotly; the terminal backend and CLI do not provide stacking.

docs.title: Scatter plots
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.mpl import plot_scatter as scatter_plot
from unrooted.core import ScatterData

sd = ScatterData(x=x_arr, y=y_arr, x_label="η", y_label="pT [GeV]")
ax = scatter_plot(sd)

Pass a HistogramStyle built with HistogramStyle.as_scatter() to control marker shape, size, color, and opacity:

from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle

style = HistogramStyle.as_scatter(marker="o", marker_size=3.0)
ax = scatter_plot(sd, style=style, label="track candidates")
ax.legend()

Or use the public overlay helper, which cycles colors and uses the first dataset's labels and title:

from unrooted.plot.mpl import overlay_scatter

ax = overlay_scatter([sd1, sd2], labels=["A", "B"])

Read point clouds through from unrooted.io.root import load_scatter.

To overlay multiple scatter datasets on the same axes, pass an existing ax:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

_, ax = plt.subplots()
scatter_plot(sd1, ax=ax, label="A", set_axis_labels=False)
scatter_plot(sd2, ax=ax, label="B", set_axis_labels=False)
ax.set_xlabel("η")
ax.legend()

docs.title: 2D histograms
docs.text:
plot() detects h.ndim == 2 automatically and renders via pcolormesh:

h2 = load("data.root", "hxy")
ax = plot(h2)

docs.title: Plotly backend
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.plotly import plot, overlay

Install the optional dependency from the source checkout first:

uv sync --extra plotly
# or
python -m pip install ".[plotly]"

The plotly backend provides a similar high-level plot() / overlay() API to the matplotlib backend, but the signatures are not identical. In particular, it returns a plotly.graph_objects.Figure instead of matplotlib axes, so matplotlib-specific parameters such as ax= are not supported, and overlay(..., ratio=True) returns a single figure rather than the (ax_main, ax_ratio) tuple returned by the matplotlib backend. Figures are interactive by default: zoom, pan, hover tooltips, and legend toggling work out of the box.

Note

Matplotlib-style shorthand colors ("C0", "r", "k") are not supported. Use hex strings ("#1A4F8A") or RGBA tuples instead.

docs.title: plot() — single histogram
docs.text:
fig = plot(h)
fig.show()                        # interactive browser window
fig.write_html("hx.html")        # self-contained interactive output
fig.write_image("hx.png")        # optional static export setup, below

Use plot(h, label="Dataset A") to override the single histogram's legend label; its name is the default. A 2D heatmap uses the axis labels and title, and does not use the 1D style settings.

Static export additionally requires Kaleido. Kaleido 1+ looks for an installed Chrome/Chromium browser; neither is included in the Plotly extra. Follow Plotly's static export instructions to configure those optional tools. HTML export does not need them.

Styled:

from unrooted.plot import HistogramStyle

fig = plot(h, style=HistogramStyle(
    line_color="#1A4F8A",
    fill_alpha=0.15,
    error_display="band",   # "bar", "band", or "continuous"
))
fig.show()

docs.title: overlay() — multiple histograms
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.plotly import overlay
from unrooted.plot import StyleSet

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")
fig = overlay(
    [h1, h2],
    labels=["signal", "background"],
    styles=[ss[0], ss[1]],
)
fig.show()

With a ratio panel:

fig = overlay([h1, h2], labels=["ref", "alt"], ratio=True)
fig.show()

docs.title: stack() — additive histogram components
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.plotly import stack

fig = stack([background_a, background_b, signal],
            labels=["Background A", "Background B", "Signal"])
fig.write_html("stack.html")

The ordering, validation, styles, missing-bin behavior, and independent total uncertainty follow the Matplotlib stack contract above. Plotly returns a Figure; it does not take ax=. Legend clicks hide a component's drawing without changing the original cumulative heights or recomputing the total uncertainty. This preserves the other components' shapes, including gaps.

Open the interactive stacked histogram.

docs.title: Scatter plots
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.plotly import plot_scatter as scatter_plot
from unrooted.core import ScatterData

sd = ScatterData(x=x_arr, y=y_arr, x_label="η", y_label="pT [GeV]")
fig = scatter_plot(sd)
fig.show()

With a custom style and label:

from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle

style = HistogramStyle.as_scatter(marker="o", marker_size=3.0).with_color("#1A4F8A")
fig = scatter_plot(sd, style=style, label="track candidates")
fig.show()

To overlay multiple datasets, use the public helper:

from unrooted.plot.plotly import overlay_scatter

fig = overlay_scatter([sd1, sd2], labels=["A", "B"])
fig.show()

For composition with other plots, plot_scatter() accepts an existing fig. Supply row and col together for a figure made with plotly.subplots.make_subplots. Labels apply only to the selected subplot; set_axis_labels=False retains the existing labels and title.

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from unrooted.plot.plotly import plot_scatter

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2)
plot_scatter(sd1, fig=fig, row=1, col=1, label="A")
plot_scatter(sd2, fig=fig, row=1, col=2, label="B")

Both scatter backends render marker settings from HistogramStyle; histogram lines, fills, error settings, and spread settings do not apply to point clouds.

docs.title: Terminal backend
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.terminal import plot, overlay

The terminal backend renders 1D histograms directly as a multi-line unicode string — no display library, no GUI, no file I/O required. Call print() on the result to display it anywhere: a notebook cell, a CI log, an SSH session.

Terminal plots require nonnegative values and render NaNs as gaps without including them in the vertical scale. Negative values raise ValueError. Overlays require exactly identical edges even without a ratio panel because the histograms share character columns. Graphical backends support negative values and ordinary overlays on different grids.

Note

Requires a monospace font with unicode support in your terminal. The plot width equals the number of bins (maximum 100).

docs.title: plot() — single histogram
docs.text:
result = plot(h, max_lines=40)
print(result)

Each bin occupies one character column; the height is proportional to the bin value scaled to max_lines rows. The y-axis shows four tick labels at 100 %, 75 %, 50 %, and 25 % of the global maximum; 0 appears on the axis line itself.

docs.text:
Up to four histograms can be overlaid. When two or more histograms are present in the same cell, a composite glyph is used:

The legend is printed below the plot when labels is supplied.

Note

Error bars and spread bands are intentionally omitted in the terminal backend — the character-cell resolution makes them impractical to render.

docs.text:
colors.json defines a four-color palette that StyleSet reads automatically:

{
  "name": "odd",
  "description": "OpenDataDetector — steel blue, vivid orange, teal/seafoam, dark crimson red",
  "colors": ["#3A6FA8", "#E8721A", "#5BB8A8", "#9B2020"]

Load it with:

from unrooted.plot import StyleSet
from unrooted.plot.mpl import plot

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")   # reads the installed ODD palette
ax = plot(h, style=ss[0])   # first of the four coordinated styles

See Styles & Themes for the full StyleSet API.

docs.title: Reading installed logo files
docs.text:
Use importlib.resources to access assets in an installed package:

from importlib.resources import as_file, files
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

logo = files("unrooted").joinpath("resources", "odd", "odd_tech_light.png")
with as_file(logo) as logo_path:
    image = plt.imread(logo_path)

The as_file context provides a filesystem path for APIs that require one. Use that path inside the context, since it may refer to a temporary file.

docs.title: Generating palette previews
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.mpl import generate_stylesheet

generate_stylesheet("odd")  # writes ./odd_stylesheet.png
generate_stylesheet("sd", "sd_preview.png")  # explicit destination

The default output is <target>_stylesheet.png in the current working directory. This replaces the previous default of writing beside the palette inside resources/<target>/. Packaged assets are read as inputs; preview generation writes to the selected destination. Its parent directory must already exist.

docs.title: Adding a new target
docs.text:
In a source checkout, create a sub-directory under unrooted/resources/ and add a colors.json with four hex codes:

{
  "name": "my_detector",
  "description": "Short description",
  "colors": ["#hex1", "#hex2", "#hex3", "#hex4"]
}

StyleSet.load("my_detector") and generate_stylesheet("my_detector") will then work in the editable development installation. Rebuild and reinstall the package to distribute the new target. Logo files are optional.

docs.title: HistogramStyle
docs.text: HistogramStyle is a dataclass that fully describes the visual appearance of a single 1D histogram. Use the named constructors for common patterns, or build the dataclass directly for full control.

docs.title: Named constructors
docs.text:
Each constructor returns a fully configured HistogramStyle and accepts **overrides to tweak individual fields:

from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle, LineStyle

# Step fill + error bars — default for count histograms
s = HistogramStyle.as_hist()

# Filled stack component + outline; uncertainty belongs to the total
s = HistogramStyle.as_stack()

# Step line only — no fill, no error display
s = HistogramStyle.as_line()

# Markers at bin centres + error bars — no step line
s = HistogramStyle.as_markers()

# Markers + error bars + spread band — suited for efficiency histograms
s = HistogramStyle.as_efficiency()

# Step line + spread band — suited for TProfile histograms
s = HistogramStyle.as_profile()

Override individual fields via keyword arguments:

s = HistogramStyle.as_line(line_style=LineStyle.DASHED, line_width=2.0)
s = HistogramStyle.as_hist(fill_alpha=0.30, error_display="band")

docs.title: with_color()
docs.text:
Apply a single color to all None color fields, returning a new instance:

from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle
from unrooted.plot.style_set import StyleSet

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")

# Fan one color out to line, fill, marker, error, and spread
style = HistogramStyle.as_hist().with_color(ss.colors[0])

# Explicitly-set colors are preserved by default
style = HistogramStyle(line_color="red").with_color("#3A6FA8")
# → line_color stays "red"; everything else is set to "#3A6FA8"

# Pass override_explicit=True to overwrite all color fields
style = HistogramStyle(line_color="red").with_color("#3A6FA8", override_explicit=True)

with_color() is the natural companion to StyleSet — it keeps the preset's shape properties while pinning a specific palette color.

docs.title: LineStyle constants
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.style import LineStyle

LineStyle.SOLID   # "-"
LineStyle.DASHED  # "--"
LineStyle.DOTTED  # ":"
LineStyle.DASHDOT # "-."

docs.title: Color fields
docs.text: All *_color fields accept any matplotlib color spec: named string ("blue"), hex ("#3A6FA8"), or RGBA tuple ((0.23, 0.44, 0.66, 1.0)). None means inherit the automatic color-cycle color.

docs.title: Line
docs.text: Field Default Effect line_color None Step-function color (None = auto cycle) line_style "-" "-", "--", ":", "-.", or None (no line) line_width 1.5 Line width in points line_alpha 1.0 Opacity

docs.title: Marker
docs.text: Field Default Effect marker None Marker at bin centres; None = no markers marker_color None Defaults to line_color marker_size 5.0 Marker size in points marker_alpha 1.0 Opacity

docs.title: Fill
docs.text: Field Default Effect fill_alpha None None = no fill; float = opacity of shaded area fill_color None Defaults to line_color fill_hatch None Hatch pattern, e.g. "/", "x", "."

docs.title: Error bars / bands
docs.text: Field Default Effect error_display "bar" "bar", "band", "continuous", or None — see display modes error_color None Defaults to line_color error_alpha 0.4 Opacity for "band" and "continuous" modes error_capsize 2.0 Cap size in points ("bar" mode only)

docs.title: Spread (profile / efficiency histograms)
docs.text: Field Default Effect spread_display None "bar", "band", "continuous", or None to show spread_min/spread_max spread_color None Defaults to line_color spread_alpha 0.15 Opacity for "band" and "continuous" modes spread_capsize 2.0 Cap size in points ("bar" mode only)

docs.title: Error and spread display modes
docs.text:
Both error_display and spread_display accept the same three modes:

Mode Description "bar" Error-bar ticks with caps drawn at each bin centre "band" Step-shaped filled area that follows the bin edges "continuous" Smooth filled envelope connecting bin centres (fill_between) 
from unrooted.plot.style import HistogramStyle
from unrooted.plot.style_set import StyleSet

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")
hist = ...  # Histogram with spread_min / spread_max (TProfile or efficiency)

# Ticks at bin centres
style_bar = HistogramStyle.as_profile(spread_display="bar").with_color(ss.colors[0])

# Step-shaped fill following bin edges
style_band = HistogramStyle.as_profile(spread_display="band").with_color(ss.colors[1])

# Smooth fill_between connecting bin centres
style_cont = HistogramStyle.as_profile(spread_display="continuous").with_color(ss.colors[2])

Choose "band" when the bin boundaries matter visually (it preserves the histogram's step structure). Choose "continuous" for a cleaner, flowing envelope — particularly useful for profile histograms with many narrow bins or when the spread is meant to represent a smooth underlying function.

docs.title: StyleSet — coordinated palettes
docs.text:
StyleSet loads a four-color palette bundled in unrooted/resources/{target}/colors.json and assembles four ready-to-use HistogramStyle objects from that palette combined with DEFAULT_STYLE_TEMPLATES.

from unrooted.plot import StyleSet

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")  # or "sd"

print(ss.name)        # "odd"
print(ss.colors)      # ['#3A6FA8', '#E8721A', '#5BB8A8', '#9B2020']
print(len(ss))        # 4

Access styles by index — indices wrap cyclically:

ss[0]   # primary    – solid line, circle marker, fill
ss[1]   # secondary  – solid line, square marker, fill
ss[2]   # tertiary   – dashed,     triangle marker, no fill
ss[3]   # quaternary – dashed,     diamond marker,  no fill
ss[4]   # same as ss[0]

docs.title: show_errors and show_spread
docs.text:
Toggle error bars and spread bands across all styles at load time:

# Disable error bars on every style
ss = StyleSet.load("odd", show_errors=False)

# Enable spread bands on every style (e.g. for a TProfile overlay)
ss = StyleSet.load("odd", show_spread=True)

docs.title: Custom StyleTemplate
docs.text:
StyleTemplate holds the shape-only properties of one slot (line style, marker, fill). Pass a custom list to override the defaults:

from unrooted.plot.style_set import StyleSet, StyleTemplate, DEFAULT_STYLE_TEMPLATES

custom = [
    StyleTemplate(line_style="-",  marker="o", fill_alpha=0.20),
    StyleTemplate(line_style="--", marker="s", fill_alpha=None),
]
ss = StyleSet.load("odd", templates=custom)

DEFAULT_STYLE_TEMPLATES is a public list you can copy and modify.

docs.title: Using with overlay()
docs.text:
from unrooted.plot.mpl import overlay
from unrooted.plot import StyleSet

ss = StyleSet.load("odd")
overlay([h1, h2, h3, h4],
        labels=["sig", "bkg", "data", "MC"],
        styles=[ss[i] for i in range(4)])
